Notes on the reporting platform migration, with particular reference to the
consistency guarantees we can and cannot offer during the transition period.

The existing reporting platform is backed by a single PostgreSQL instance with a
read replica used exclusively for analytical queries, and the replication is
asynchronous, which means that the replica may lag behind the primary by an
interval that varies with write volume and which we have observed to reach
several seconds during the end-of-month batch window. Any migration strategy
that reads from the replica must therefore account for the possibility that a
record written to the primary immediately prior to the cutover has not yet
propagated, and that a naive comparison between source and destination will
report a spurious discrepancy.

The archive transfer is the more tractable of the two stages, since the
historical partitions are immutable once the month has closed, and consequently
a checksum computed over a closed partition on the source will match a checksum
computed over the corresponding partition on the destination provided that the
serialisation format has been preserved exactly. It is worth noting that the
serialisation format has not in fact been preserved exactly across the two
previous platform upgrades, because the timestamp columns were migrated from a
timezone-naive representation to a timezone-aware one, and the conversion was
performed with an assumed offset that was correct for the majority of records
but incorrect for those written during the two weeks following each daylight
saving transition.

The live reporting transfer is considerably more difficult, because the
reporting functions are not idempotent. A report generated twice against the
same underlying data will produce two entries in the audit log, and the
downstream reconciliation process treats a duplicated audit entry as evidence of
a failed run, which triggers a retry, which produces a third entry. This
behaviour has been documented since the original implementation but has never
been exercised in production because the scheduler has never been run
concurrently against the same dataset.

My recommendation is that we introduce an idempotency key derived from the
report parameters and the logical reporting date, that we store it in the audit
table with a unique constraint, and that we treat a constraint violation as a
successful no-op rather than as an error. This is a small change and it can be
deployed independently of the migration, which seems to me the strongest
argument in its favour: it reduces the risk of the migration without being
coupled to it.

There is a secondary consideration regarding the reconciliation scripts
themselves. They are written in a mixture of shell and awk, they depend on the
column ordering of the source tables rather than on column names, and they will
therefore break silently rather than loudly if the destination schema differs in
ordering. I would suggest that we regenerate them against column names before
the migration rather than after, on the grounds that a silent failure discovered
in January is considerably more expensive than a noisy one discovered now.
